notes.body:
The doctrinal principle that bridges those hierarchical figures and those practical obligations is the Ismaili teaching of the divine degrees (حدود): every rank in the spiritual hierarchy has an active counterpart in the believer's personal religion. The connection between the seven Imams and the **seven obligations**, or between the twelve proofs and the twelve practices, is structural, not incidental.

The seven Imams recur in the world like the days of the week because they represent the complete, unbroken presence of Allah's guidance across every age and cycle. Each of the seven obligations corresponds to one dimension of that living presence, and they begin with **guardianship** (ولاية) because it is the root from which every other obligation draws its meaning. Prayer, fasting, and pilgrimage are themselves forms of that love, made visible.

The twelve proofs (حجج) are spread throughout the world as the Imam's ambassadors, sustaining the community's moral and social fabric wherever they reach. The twelve incumbent practices are exactly that fabric, as the believer lives it from within:

- Honoring parents and maintaining kinship ties
- Protecting neighbors and enjoining what is good
- Forbidding what is wrong, feeding others, visiting the sick

These are not courtesies added on top of religion; they are the **hierarchy enacted in daily life**, rippling outward from the Imam's light through the proofs and into every household.

The key that binds the two levels together is the Ismaili principle of the outward (ظاهر) and the inward (باطن). The seven Imams and twelve proofs are the inner, hierarchical reality; the seven obligations and twelve practices are their outer expression in time. This is why the text insists so firmly: without **both knowledge and action**, the name of faith cannot rightly apply.

etymology: حدود (divine degrees): from the root ح-د-د, meaning to be sharp, to mark a precise boundary. A حدّ is the exact edge where one thing ends and another begins — like a blade's cutting edge. The حدود are the sharply defined ranks of the spiritual hierarchy, each marking exactly where one degree of being ends and a higher one begins.

ولاية (guardianship): from the root و-ل-ي, meaning to be near, to be adjacent, to take charge. A وليّ is one close enough to act on your behalf. The ولاية is nearness made covenant: the Imam is near to Allah, and the believer draws near to the Imam, forming a chain of proximity from the divine all the way down to us.

حجة (proof): from the root ح-ج-ج — the same root as pilgrimage (حجّ) — meaning to go toward, to visit, to overcome in argument. The حجة is the one who overcomes doubt by his very presence — the living argument that Allah's guidance has never been withdrawn from the world.

ظاهر (outward): from the root ظ-ه-ر, meaning to appear, to rise above the surface — as the sun rises (ظَهَرَ). The ظاهر is whatever is visible and accessible, the outer face of religion. The same root gives ظَهْر, the back — the surface others see when facing you.

باطن (inward): from the root ب-ط-ن, meaning to lie inside, to be hidden within — as the belly (بَطْن) is hidden inside the body. The باطن is the concealed meaning the outer form protects. The same root gives بطانة, the lining of a garment: invisible, but essential to its structure.

notes.body:
The silence on justification is itself meaningful. In Ismaili jurisprudence, authoritative teaching (تعليم) — **the Imam's own knowledge transmitted through his chain of callers** — is itself the proof; no Quranic verse or named hadith needs appending. The readers of this text were members of the call (دعوة), accepting a ruling on the strength of who transmitted it, tracing back through the callers (الدعاة) to the Imam himself.

The exemption of women becomes clearer when we see what the twelve practices correspond to. They map onto the twelve proofs (الحجج) scattered across the world — the regional pillars of the دعوة hierarchy. In the Tayyibi دعوة of this era, that was a public, institutional role held by men; the twelve obligations belong to **a specific institutional office**, not to every believer equally.

Several items on the list presuppose a male, institutionally-positioned agent:

- "Good conduct with one's spouse" addresses a husband, not a spouse in the abstract.
- "Keeping the bond among the brethren" implies the fraternal network of the دعوة.
- "Enjoining what is good and forbidding what is wrong" carries a public dimension tied to social authority and position.

Women are not exempt from **the spirit** of these acts — they are exempt from the formal obligation attached to that institutional office.

A caller (داعي) transmits doctrine rather than constructing arguments from scratch; the chain (سلسلة) of Imams and callers **is itself the only authority that matters** — the book's opening pages name that chain, and in naming it, they answer the question the reader is asking.
notes.anchor: These twelve are not obligatory upon women.
notes.quote: These twelve are not obligatory upon women.
etymology: تعليم (authoritative teaching): from the root ع-ل-م, meaning to know or to mark something with a sign. The verb علّم means to teach — to plant a mark of knowledge in another. In Ismaili doctrine, تعليم is not casual instruction but Imam-sourced transmission: the knowledge is valid only through its living source, so teacher and truth are inseparable.

حجة (proof / regional representative): from the root ح-ج-ج, meaning to intend purposefully or to overcome in argument. The pilgrimage (الحج) shares this root — a directed journey toward a centre. A حجة is a proof that defeats doubt, and in the دعوة hierarchy it names the Imam's regional representative: a person who embodies the living argument for the Imam's authority.

دعوة (the call): from the root د-ع-و, meaning to call out or to invite. To make a دعوة is to extend an invitation across a distance. In Ismaili tradition, the دعوة is the institution through which the Imam's guidance reaches the world, each caller (داعي) extending that invitation to those with ears willing to hear.

سلسلة (chain of transmission): from the root س-ل-س-ل, whose repeated syllables mimic the interlocking of links. A سلسلة is a chain in which each link depends on the one before it. In Ismaili doctrine, the chain's authority rests entirely on the integrity of its first link — the Imam himself, from whom all knowledge originally flows.
